readings.title: The return of shade to a city street
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A city planted trees along a busy shopping street to make summer walks more comfortable. The first plan placed identical trees at regular distances. It looked tidy on paper, but a survey of the street revealed several difficulties. Delivery vehicles needed room to stop, an underground cable crossed one section, and two shop windows relied on daylight. The planning team walked the route with shopkeepers, residents and maintenance workers before marking final planting sites.

Instead of abandoning the project, the team selected three kinds of trees that would grow to different sizes. Smaller trees went near the shop windows, while larger ones were placed where people waited for buses. The team also left a clear path wide enough for wheelchairs and pushchairs. Each planting site had to be checked for pipes and cables. These changes meant fewer trees than originally proposed, but the ones planted had a better chance of surviving.

During the first summer, the city measured the temperature of several shaded and unshaded places at the same time of day. People standing under the young trees reported feeling more comfortable, although the recorded difference was still small. The team reminded residents that young trees would not provide full shade immediately. Regular watering and protection from damage were essential. A nearby school volunteered to help record whether the trees remained healthy, but trained workers kept responsibility for maintenance.

Three years later, the city planned to compare the street again, including how easy it was to walk, wait and shop there. Planting was only the beginning of the project. Its value would depend on whether the trees could grow safely alongside the many activities already taking place on the street. Residents would be invited to report damage through an existing public service line.
knowledgePoints: 阅读理解：城市环境与规划

readings.title: An evening class learns from errors
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
In an evening mathematics class, several adults were reluctant to show their work. They had returned to study after years away from school and feared that a wrong answer would waste everyone's time. Their teacher noticed that students often copied the final answer without understanding the steps. She decided to change how the group discussed mistakes. Once a week, she presented a solution containing an error that she had written herself. Students worked in pairs to identify the step where the reasoning changed direction.

At first, the class focused on finding the incorrect number. The teacher then asked a second question: what reasonable thought might have led someone to make that choice? Students began to explain why a method looked attractive and where it stopped working. This reduced the feeling that an error was simply a sign of carelessness. It also gave the teacher information about which ideas needed further explanation.

After a month, learners could choose to discuss one of their own attempts anonymously. The teacher never required anyone to reveal a personal mistake. One student submitted a problem about percentages that many classmates had found difficult. Their discussion showed that the class needed more practice distinguishing a percentage of a total from a percentage change. The next lesson used prices and wages to make the distinction clearer.

Scores on a short classroom exercise improved, but the teacher considered another change equally important. More students were willing to ask how an answer had been reached. She still gave direct feedback and expected accurate work. Her aim was to make the path to accuracy visible. For these learners, discussing a mistaken step in a respectful way became a tool for understanding, rather than a public judgment about ability. Several learners began keeping notes about methods they wanted to revisit.

readings.title: A market tries reusable containers
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
The owners of a weekend food market wanted to reduce the number of disposable containers left in nearby bins. They considered requiring every seller to use one standard reusable box. Some sellers welcomed the idea, but others sold food that needed different packaging. Customers also arrived from many places, making it uncertain whether they could return a box the following week. The market committee therefore began with a smaller trial at four stalls.

Customers at those stalls could pay a small deposit for a sturdy container and return it to any participating stall. A printed card explained how the deposit worked. At the end of each market day, the committee counted containers issued and returned. It also asked sellers how much time they spent washing and storing them. The first two weeks produced mixed results. Many containers came back, but customers sometimes forgot that a return was possible at a different stall. Some also believed the deposit was an extra charge for their meal.

The committee improved the signs and trained stall workers to give the same brief explanation. It arranged a shared washing area so that individual sellers did not need to carry containers home. Returns increased, yet the group continued to record difficulties. In particular, it needed to know whether the washing process used more water than expected. It compared the trial with the previous packaging system instead of claiming an environmental benefit from appearance alone.

At the end of three months, the committee chose to expand the trial gradually. It published the figures it had collected and invited feedback from sellers who had not joined. The system was not suitable for every kind of food. Still, the trial showed that a practical environmental change often depends on clear instructions, convenient returns and honest measurement of hidden costs. Future reports would include both customer experience and water use.

readings.title: The value of a neighbourhood repair record
readings.instruction: Read the passage and choose the best answer to each question.
readings.content:
A group of volunteers offered a monthly repair afternoon for small household objects. At first, they wrote down only how many objects had been fixed. Their records suggested that success was growing, because more people came each month. Yet the volunteers noticed that some visitors returned with the same problem. They also spent a great deal of time on items that were unsafe to repair without special training. To understand the service better, the group changed its record sheet.

The new sheet included the type of object, the problem described by its owner and the result of the visit. Volunteers could mark an item as repaired, partly repaired or referred to a professional. They noted when a visitor learned a simple maintenance step that might prevent the problem from returning. Names were not required for this record, and the group explained why the information was being collected.

After several months, the records showed that a loose electrical connection was a common reason for visits. The group did not respond by asking untrained volunteers to fix more electrical items. Instead, it arranged a short safety talk from a qualified technician and printed advice about when professional help was necessary. It also discovered that many bicycle problems involved tyres that were not kept at the correct pressure. A brief demonstration helped owners check them safely.

The number of objects repaired remained useful, but it no longer told the whole story. A referral could protect a visitor from harm, and a small lesson could prevent another fault. The group published a summary without identifying owners. By recording what happened and what people learned, the volunteers could improve the service while staying within the limits of their skills. Visitors could also use that summary to prepare questions before attending.

translation.stem:
Translate the following passage into Chinese:
A useful record should help a group make better decisions, not merely produce a large number. When volunteers describe what happened during each visit, they can see which problems return and which tasks require expert help. They should also explain why they collect information and avoid writing down details that are unnecessary for their purpose. A short summary can show the public what the service has learned without exposing individual visitors. Over time, these records may reveal whether a change has made work safer or more effective. If the results are mixed, the group can adjust its approach and continue to learn.
translation.explanation: 注意not merely、which引导的定语从句及whether表示的是否。
translation.referenceAnswer: 有用的记录应帮助团队作出更好的决定，而不只是得出一个大数字。志愿者描述每次来访的情况时，就能看出哪些问题反复出现，哪些任务需要专业帮助。他们还应解释收集信息的原因，并避免记下与目的无关的细节。一份简短的总结既能向公众展示服务学到了什么，又不会泄露个别访客的信息。随着时间推移，这些记录或许能说明某项改变是否使工作更安全或更有效。如果结果好坏参半，团队可以调整方法并继续学习。

writing.stem: Write at least 100 words in English to a neighbourhood association proposing an activity that helps residents learn about local nature. Explain what people would do, how you would make the activity accessible, and how the association could learn from participants comments.
writing.explanation: 范文覆盖活动内容、可参与性和收集反馈三个要点。
writing.sampleAnswer:
Dear Association Members,
I would like to suggest a monthly nature walk along the river. Volunteers could help residents notice common birds, plants and changes in the water. Participants would record observations in a simple notebook, but no previous knowledge would be required.
To make the walk accessible, the route should be short and clearly described in advance. We could offer both a morning and an evening session, and provide a printed summary for anyone who cannot attend. A meeting point near the bus stop would help people without a car.
After each walk, participants could share one thing they learned and one difficulty they faced. The association could use these comments to adjust the route or timing. A short public summary would also show how the activity is developing.
Yours sincerely,
A resident
